prompt: Why does the course recommend building the lab inside a virtual machine rather than on your own computer?
hint: Think about what the script does as root.

choices.text: Because containers booted under a hypervisor run faster than on the bare computer
choices.why: They do not: a hypervisor adds a layer, it does not speed anything up.

choices.text: Because Ubuntu 24.04 cannot be installed on a laptop
choices.why: It can; installed is one of the three paths, for a computer you can wipe.

choices.text: Because each of the seven machines needs its own access to the internet
choices.why: The opposite: the seven machines are on a network connected to nothing.

choices.text: Because it changes the computer as root, and a VM is deleted whole
choices.why: Right. Namespaces, containers and 7 GB under /var/lib/hostlab go away with the virtual machine.

prompt: A student opens a Linux shell in a browser tab offered by a website and tries to build the lab there. What happens, and why?
hint: What is the lab made of?

choices.text: It works, only more slowly, because every container is nested inside the website's own
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; the operations themselves are refused.

choices.text: It works once and then the website deletes it
choices.why: It never gets that far: creating the containers fails.

choices.text: It fails: that shell is already a container
choices.why: Right. The lab is containers and network namespaces, which need root on a real or virtual machine.

choices.text: It fails, because a browser tab has no way to run bash
choices.why: The shell runs on the website's server, not in the browser; bash is there.

prompt: Before running hostlab.sh for the first time, what does the lesson ask you to compare?
hint: A script that runs as root deserves a look.

choices.text: Its checksum and its number of lines
choices.why: Right. If either differs, the copy lost or gained something.

choices.text: Its file name and location with the ones the lesson uses in its own transcripts
choices.why: A name can match while the content is wrong.

choices.text: The version of bash on your computer with the one the course was recorded with
choices.why: The script runs on any bash Ubuntu 24.04 ships; the content is what can go wrong.

choices.text: The size of the two images in /var/lib/hostlab after the build has finished
choices.why: That comes after running it, which is exactly what the check is meant to precede.

prompt: You changed a file on web in lesson 1. You type `sudo bash hostlab.sh up` at the start of lesson 2. Where is your change?

choices.text: Still on web, because up only starts machines that are stopped
choices.why: up stops every machine first and makes fresh copies.

choices.text: In the web image, saved there by up for the lessons after it
choices.why: Changes happen in the copy, never in the image.

choices.text: Gone: up replaces every copy with a new one
choices.why: Right. Every lesson starts from the same place as its transcripts.

prompt: `sudo bash hostlab.sh up` answers `set: pipefail^M: invalid option name`. What is the cause?

choices.text: The installed bash is too old to know pipefail
choices.why: Ubuntu 24.04's bash knows it; the error names the option with something stuck to it.

choices.text: The file has Windows line endings
choices.why: Right. ^M is the carriage return, and sed -i "s/\r$//" removes it.

choices.text: The script was run without sudo, so bash refused its first option
choices.why: Without sudo it says so in plain words: run it with sudo, from your own account.

choices.text: The images were never built
choices.why: That message names build; this one fails before any of the script's own checks run.

prompt: After up, one machine prints `degraded`. Where do you look first?

choices.text: At the lab computer's own firewall
choices.why: The lab is not connected to the computer's network; nothing there affects a service inside a machine.

choices.text: At build.log, from the start
choices.why: build.log tells you how the image was made; the machine can tell you what failed now.

choices.text: At `systemctl --failed` on that machine, then journalctl for the unit it names
choices.why: Right. degraded means a unit failed, and those two commands name it and say why.

prompt: Which of these is part of a server's attack surface?
hint: Something a stranger could reach or use.

choices.text: The length of its host name, which a scan reports
choices.why: A name is not something anyone can talk to or log in with.

choices.text: An FTP server nobody uses, still listening
choices.why: Right. Every listener is a program a stranger can talk to without logging in.

choices.text: The amount of free space on its disk
choices.why: Disk space matters to availability, but nobody reaches the machine through it.

choices.text: The firewall on the network in front of it
choices.why: That is a control in front of the surface, not part of it.

prompt: A UDP scan reports `5353/udp open|filtered`. What does nmap actually know?

choices.text: That a firewall dropped the probe
choices.why: That is one of the two explanations, and nmap cannot tell which.

choices.text: That avahi is running and answered
choices.why: An answer would have made it open; here nothing came back.

choices.text: Only that no reply came back
choices.why: Right. The machine itself, with ss, settles it.

choices.text: That the port is closed and nothing listens there
choices.why: Closed is a reply; the after-scan shows it as closed.

prompt: The first scan of web found five TCP and three UDP services. The portal's job needs two. How many listeners had no reason to be there?
ss shows `tcp 127.0.0.1:8080 python3`. Who can connect to it?

choices.text: Only programs on web itself, such as nginx
choices.why: Right. The loopback address never leaves the machine.

choices.text: Every machine on the 192.168.60.0/24 segment
choices.why: That would be 0.0.0.0 or web's own address.

choices.text: Anybody on the internet, unless a firewall blocks it
choices.why: Loopback is unreachable from outside with or without a firewall.

choices.text: Only root, because the port is above 1024
choices.why: Ports below 1024 need root to listen on, and nothing restricts who connects.

prompt: After `systemctl disable --now rpcbind`, port 111 is still open, held by systemd. What is holding it, and how do you close it?

choices.text: A zombie rpcbind process; kill it with kill -9
choices.why: No rpcbind process is left: ss names systemd, process 1.

choices.text: The kernel caches the port for a minute; wait
choices.why: Nothing expires here: systemd is listening on purpose and would start rpcbind again.

choices.text: A socket unit, which has to be switched off as well
choices.why: Right. systemd listens for the service and starts it on the first connection.

choices.text: inetd, which starts rpcbind whenever a client asks; remove inetd first
choices.why: inetd ran telnet here; the warning names rpcbind.socket.

prompt: Match each way of switching a service off with what it leaves behind.

pairs.right: installed, and startable by hand or by another unit
installed, and linked to /dev/null so nothing can start it
neither the program nor its configuration

right_distractors: the program, with its configuration reset to defaults

prompt: You inherit a server and find an FTP service that seems idle. What should happen before you purge it?
hint: The service may have a user you do not know about.

choices.text: Nothing: an idle service is unnecessary by definition
choices.why: Idle today is not idle on the day the monthly job runs.

choices.text: Find out who uses it, and write the answer down
choices.why: Right. And the note answers the next person who finds FTP missing.

choices.text: Disable it for a whole year first, and purge it only if nobody has complained by then
choices.why: A year of a disabled service still answers nothing about who needed it.

choices.text: Upgrade it, so that it is safe to keep
choices.why: A patched service nobody needs is still surface.

prompt: Why is an account called `suporte` with user id 0 a problem even though it is not called root?

choices.text: Because the kernel checks the number, not the name
choices.why: Right. It is root under another name, with its own password.

choices.text: Because two accounts may not share the same home directory, and /root belongs to root
choices.why: Sharing a home is untidy; the danger is the number.

choices.text: Because Portuguese names break sudo
choices.why: Names are just labels; nothing breaks.

choices.text: Because only root may have a password
choices.why: Any account may have one; what this one has is root's powers.

prompt: A colleague suggests `userdel -rf suporte` to remove the second root. What would it do on web?
hint: Look at the home directory of suporte.

choices.text: Remove the name and nothing else, which is what you want
choices.why: -r does more than the name: it removes the home directory.

choices.text: Fail, exactly as plain userdel did
choices.why: -f overrides the check that stopped the plain command.

choices.text: Delete /root, which is suporte's home
choices.why: Right. The safe removal deletes the account's lines from the four account files.

choices.text: Lock the account, which leaves it in place for the logs to name
choices.why: That is usermod -L; userdel removes.

prompt: Which changes stop the intern's account from logging in? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: usermod -L, which locks the password
choices.why: A locked password cannot be used to log in.

choices.text: usermod -e 1, which makes the account expired
choices.why: An expired account is refused whatever the password.

choices.text: usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin, which takes its shell away
choices.why: nologin prints a refusal and exits.

choices.text: chage -l estagio, which shows its dates
choices.why: chage -l only reads; it changes nothing.

prompt: /etc/sudoers.d has no file for an account, yet it can use sudo. Where does that power come from?
hint: A list that is not in /etc/passwd.

choices.text: Membership of the sudo group, which getent group sudo lists
choices.why: Right. getent group sudo lists everybody who may use it.

choices.text: Its SSH key in authorized_keys
choices.why: A key lets it log in; it grants no privilege after that.

choices.text: A user id below 1000
choices.why: Low ids are system accounts by convention, with no sudo rights.

choices.text: Its login shell being /bin/bash
choices.why: A shell lets it log in interactively; sudo checks groups and rules.

prompt: `50-old.conf` says `PermitRootLogin yes`. You add `90-hardening.conf` saying `PermitRootLogin no` and reload. What does `sshd -T` report?
hint: Which file is read first, and which value does sshd keep?

choices.text: permitrootlogin no, because the newest file wins
choices.why: File age plays no part; the order is by name.

choices.text: permitrootlogin yes, because 50 is read before 90 and sshd keeps the first value
choices.why: Right. That is why the lesson named the file 10-hardening.conf.

choices.text: An error, because a setting may only appear once
choices.why: Repeating it is allowed; only the first value counts.

choices.text: permitrootlogin no, because no is always safer
choices.why: sshd does not pick the safer value, it picks the first one.

prompt: Why does the lesson run `sshd -t` before `systemctl reload ssh`?
hint: What happens if the configuration has a typo?

choices.text: To print the settings the server would run with
choices.why: That is sshd -T, with a capital T.

choices.text: To restart the server without dropping sessions
choices.why: -t starts nothing; reload is what keeps sessions.

choices.text: To test a login with the new settings from another machine
choices.why: That is the next step, from desk.

choices.text: To catch a typo before it reaches the running server
choices.why: Right. The && means reload runs only if the check passed.

prompt: Match each SSH setting with what it closes.

pairs.right: the one account name every attacker knows
guessing a password from anywhere the port is reachable
graphical programs tunnelled from a server with no screen
many attempts inside a single connection

prompt: `apt-cache rdepends --installed wpasupplicant` lists nothing under it on web. What does that tell you?

choices.text: That no installed package needs it
choices.why: Right. Whether the machine's job needs it is the other half of the question.

choices.text: That wpasupplicant is not installed on web, so there is nothing to remove
choices.why: It is installed, and running; the command asked who needs it.

choices.text: That it has no security updates
choices.why: Dependencies say nothing about updates.

choices.text: That the machine has a Wi-Fi card
choices.why: Packages know nothing about hardware; web has no radio.

prompt: After `server_tokens off`, what has the portal gained?

choices.text: Protection against the flaws in nginx 1.24.0
choices.why: A hidden version is just as vulnerable; lesson 16 finds out which are out of date.

choices.text: A server that no longer tells anybody it is nginx at all
choices.why: The name stays; only the version goes.

choices.text: Its version number is no longer announced to whoever asks
choices.why: Right. It is a small change and not a fix.

choices.text: Faster responses, because the header is shorter
choices.why: A few bytes make no difference anybody can measure here.

prompt: Put in order the way this lesson hardens a service you did not install.
items: scan the machine from another one on the network
ask the machine which process holds each port
find out whether anybody uses the service
remove the service and its socket
scan again from the same machine

prompt: The final UDP scan reports 161/udp as `closed` where it first said `open`. What made the difference visible to nmap?
hint: Closed is an answer, not a silence.

choices.text: snmpd now drops the probes it receives
choices.why: snmpd is gone; nothing on the port receives anything.

choices.text: web's kernel answers that no program listens there
choices.why: Right. With nothing listening the kernel replies port unreachable, which nmap reads as closed.

choices.text: A firewall was added to web during the lesson
choices.why: No firewall was added in this lesson; that is lesson 5.

choices.text: The community string was changed from public
choices.why: The service was purged, not reconfigured.

prompt: A service account gets the shell /usr/sbin/___, which prints a refusal and exits.
How many packages did web lose in this lesson, counting the service packages and the two Wi-Fi ones?
Which of these reduce web's attack surface, rather than protect what is already there? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Purging the telnet server
choices.why: A program that is not there has nothing to attack.

choices.text: Watching the FTP logs for failed logins
choices.why: That guards a service that is still there.

choices.text: Removing the second account with user id 0
choices.why: One less way in, and a powerful one.

choices.text: Choosing a longer password for the intern
choices.why: The account still exists and still logs in; the lesson locked it instead.
